why.correct: The protein with lower identity (46%) restores growth while one with higher identity (58%) does not, so identity alone cannot be what decides success. Something else, such as fitting into a complex with yeast partner proteins, matters too.
options: Correct: lower identity succeeds and higher identity fails, which identity alone cannot explain.
Both have fairly high identity and both work, which fits the idea that identity predicts success.
Both fail, so this pair cannot show that identity is a poor predictor; the 31% protein failing is what identity would predict.
Both work at similar identity, so the pair fits identity as a predictor.

why.correct: The human gene is read with the same genetic code by yeast's ribosomes, and the enzyme it codes for still does the same job because both versions descend from one ancestral enzyme. Common ancestry explains both the shared code and the shared function.
options: Correct: a shared code lets yeast translate the gene, and shared descent keeps the enzyme's function.
Mutations are random and rare; nothing steers a gene toward the yeast sequence within 48 hours.
Only 53% of the amino acids are identical, so the proteins differ at nearly half their positions.
Separate origins would not explain why the human enzyme works inside yeast, or why the sequences match at over half their positions.

why.correct: Strains given their own gene back grow at 97-101% of normal, so the procedure itself does not harm growth. When a human gene fails (0%), the failure must come from the human gene, not from the method.
options: Correct: it shows the method works, so a failure points to the gene put in.
The no-gene control (0% growth) is what shows the gene is needed; putting the yeast gene back does not test that.
This control uses yeast genes, so it says nothing about translating human genes.
Unaltered yeast and the put-back strains grow well in the same medium, but that is not the main thing this control is designed to test.

why.correct: 61% of positions are identical, so 100% − 61% = 39% differ. 0.39 × 200 = 78 positions. The protein still works in yeast despite 78 differences, which suggests many positions can change without destroying function, while the identical ones are likely the essential ones.
Shared genes that still work in each other's cells show descent from a common ancestor. Both lineages have kept changing since they split, so neither modern organism is the ancestor of the other.
options: Correct: shared ancestry, not descent of one living organism from another.
Working genes show both inherited them from a common ancestor; modern yeast has evolved for as long as the human line has.
Failures are expected where proteins have changed or must work with partners that changed; most of the genes still worked.
About half the amino acids differ, which fits a very distant relationship, not a close one.

why.correct: X has no nucleus, so it is a prokaryote, and its ether-linked lipids, histones and lack of peptidoglycan mark it as an archaeon.
options: Correct: no nucleus plus ether-linked lipids and histones fit Archaea.
Z has ester-linked lipids and no histones, like the bacterium W; its missing wall is not enough to make it an archaeon.
W has no nucleus, so it cannot be a eukaryote.
Y has a nucleus, linear chromosomes and introns, so it is a eukaryote.

why.correct: A feature can show that all four share an ancestor only if all four have it. The genetic code and membrane ATP synthase are found in all four, as in all known life.
options: Shared by all four: the same code points to one origin.
Shared by all four: the same ATP-making machine points to one origin.
W and Z lack histones, so this feature cannot link all four.
Only X has ether-linked lipids.
Y's chromosome is linear, so this feature does not unite all four.

why.correct: A newer feature that two organisms share, and others lack, points to an ancestor they alone share. Histone-wrapped DNA is such a feature: X and Y have it, W does not.
options: Correct: a shared newer feature unites X and Y.
Lacking a nucleus is the older state that all prokaryotes keep, so it links X to W no more than it links X to any prokaryote.
Lacking a feature is weak evidence: Z, which matches the bacterium W in its lipids and lack of histones, also lacks peptidoglycan.
A circular chromosome is the older state shared by all prokaryotes, so it does not show that X and W are close.

why.correct: Penicillin can only harm cells that build peptidoglycan. In the table, W is the one with a peptidoglycan wall.
options: Z is a bacterium by its other features, but it has no peptidoglycan wall, so penicillin has nothing to block.
Correct: W is the one organism making peptidoglycan.
Neither X nor Y makes peptidoglycan.
X and Z lack peptidoglycan; being prokaryotes does not make them sensitive.

why.correct: Y has a nucleus and genes with introns, so its RNA transcripts are spliced before translation. W has neither, so its mRNA can be translated as it is made.
options: Correct: splicing needs introns, which W lacks.
Translation by ribosomes happens in every cell.
Every cell transcribes its genes with an RNA polymerase.
Every cell starts translation at a start codon; it is part of the shared genetic code.

why.correct: A nucleus wrapped in a double membrane is one of the features eukaryotes share with each other and not with Bacteria or Archaea. (Linear chromosomes are a eukaryote feature too, but a few bacteria also have them.)
options: Correct: prokaryotes keep their DNA in the cytoplasm, with no nucleus around it.
Ribosomes are in every cell, prokaryote or eukaryote.
Every cell is bounded by a plasma membrane.
DNA is the genetic material of every cell.

why.correct: Which codon stands for which amino acid is largely arbitrary, and a change to the code would alter many proteins at once, so a code, once in place, is kept. The same code everywhere is best explained by inheritance from one ancestor.
options: Correct: an arbitrary code shared by all is best explained by shared descent.
Engineered and natural variant codes work, so chemistry does not force this code; if it did, sharing it would say nothing about ancestry.
Genes move between organisms, but the code is read by a cell's own tRNAs and enzymes and is not swapped as a unit.
The code is very stable, which is why it is shared by organisms whose last common ancestor lived billions of years ago.

why.correct: These variant codes differ from the standard code in only a few of the 64 codons (two in the ciliates, four in human mitochondria). Small changes in a code that is otherwise identical are what descent with modification predicts.
options: Correct: tiny departures from one shared code point to modification after shared descent.
Separate origins would give codes unlike each other throughout, not codes that match at nearly all 64 codons.
Nearly identical codes still point to shared descent; small changes after inheritance are expected.
A shared code is one of the strongest lines of evidence for common ancestry.

why.correct: Features that Archaea and eukaryotes share and Bacteria lack, such as a complex RNA polymerase and histones, point to an ancestor that Archaea and eukaryotes alone share.
options: Correct: shared newer features link Archaea with eukaryotes.
Lacking a nucleus is the older condition of all prokaryotes, so it does not show that Archaea and Bacteria are close.
Where an organism lives says little about whom it shares an ancestor with.
Ribosome size is an older shared feature of prokaryotes and does not group Archaea with Bacteria more closely.

why.correct: H4 is a conserved protein: mutations arise in its gene as in any gene, but almost every amino acid change harms DNA packing, so natural selection removes it. Over a billion or so years, very few changes have survived.
options: Correct: selection removes harmful changes, keeping the sequence nearly the same.
Mutations arise in this gene at a normal rate; what differs is that selection removes most changes to the protein.
Plants and animals last shared an ancestor over a billion years ago, which is plenty of time for change.
H4 is a protein, built from amino acids.

why.correct: A conserved gene is not one that mutates less. Its mutations arise at the usual rate, but those that change the protein are removed by selection, so amino acid differences stay few while silent differences build up as in any gene.

variables.name: Number of amino acid differences between the mouse and human proteins
variables.why: Most amino acid changes in F harm the ribosome and are removed by selection, so fewer differences remain than in P.

variables.name: Rate at which new mutations arise in the gene's DNA
variables.why: Mutations arise by chance at similar rates in both genes; what differs is which mutations are kept.

variables.name: Share of amino acid-changing mutations that persist over many generations
variables.why: Carriers of most F changes have lower fitness, so those mutations are lost more often than changes in P.

variables.name: Number of silent base differences that leave the amino acid unchanged
variables.why: Silent changes do not alter the protein, so selection does not remove them faster in F than in P; both genes collect them at similar rates.

why.correct: LUCA is the latest ancestor shared by all life today. Life had probably existed for some time before it, and LUCA already had DNA, the genetic code and ribosomes.
options: Correct: the latest shared ancestor, not the first life.
LUCA was not necessarily the first life; other early lineages may have existed and left no descendants.
LUCA lived billions of years ago; no organism alive today is the ancestor of the others.
Bacteria and Archaea have no nucleus; the nucleus arose later, in the eukaryote line.

why.correct: Common ancestry is judged from many features together. Bacteria and Archaea share the deep, arbitrary features of all life, and a difference in one feature is expected to arise in one line after the split.
options: Correct: many shared core features outweigh one later change.
The lipids really do differ (ester versus ether links); lacking a nucleus is an older shared state, not proof of one group.
Lipids are made by enzymes, and enzymes are coded by genes, so lipid differences do reflect genes.
There is no evidence that Archaea got their lipids from eukaryotes.

why.correct: Mitochondria arose from an engulfed bacterium and kept bacteria-like ribosomes. Shared ancestry with bacteria explains why drugs aimed at bacterial ribosomes can also affect them.
options: Correct: mitochondrial ribosomes inherited bacterial features.
Most of a cell's proteins are made on cytoplasmic ribosomes; mitochondria make a few of their own.
Nothing suggests these drugs become hormones; the effect comes from binding ribosomes.
Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are larger and differ from bacterial ones, which is why these drugs spare most human protein synthesis.

why.correct: Eukaryotes inherited a shared set of features from their common ancestor, including introns and membrane-bound organelles, so a new eukaryote is predicted to have them.
options: Introns and splicing are shared eukaryotic features.
Membrane-bound organelles define eukaryotic cells.
Peptidoglycan walls are a bacterial feature.
Ether-linked lipids are the archaeal kind; eukaryotes use ester links.
Eukaryotes have linear chromosomes wrapped on histones.

why.correct: Year-by-year rises: 3 to 4, 21 to 34 (13 points); 4 to 5, 34 to 48 (14 points); 5 to 6, 48 to 60 (12 points); 7 to 8, 68 to 72 (4 points). The largest is from year 4 to year 5.
options: A rise of 13 points, close but one point less than from year 4 to year 5.
Correct: 48 − 34 = 14 percentage points, the largest single-year rise.
A rise of 12 points; the climb was already slowing.
A rise of 4 points; by then the curve had nearly leveled off.

why.correct: From 12% in year 2 to 60% in year 6: (60 − 12) ÷ (6 − 2) = 48 ÷ 4 = 12.0 percentage points per year.

Variation comes first: the allele existed by chance before the insecticide arrived. The insecticide killed susceptible mosquitoes more often, so carriers left more offspring and the allele's frequency rose.
options: Correct: random mutation supplies the allele; selection by the insecticide raises its frequency.
Mutations are not produced on demand by the environment; the allele was present in year 0, before any nets.
Changes during an individual's life are not inherited; the sodium-channel gene itself must carry the change.
Nets carry no mosquitoes or genes; the allele was in the local population before the nets arrived.

why.correct: Without pyrethroid the allele's benefit is gone but its small cost remains, so carriers leave slightly fewer offspring each generation and the frequency drifts down slowly, not instantly.
options: Correct: a small cost with no benefit means slow decline.
The stem says carriers survive slightly less well without pyrethroid, so the allele is no longer neutral.
Allele frequencies change across generations through differences in reproduction; individuals cannot switch their alleles off.
The new insecticide acts on a different target, so kdr gives no extra protection against it.

why.correct: Without a comparison district, the rise could come from something else that changed, such as crop spraying with the same insecticide. A similar district without nets, where kdr stays low, would tie the rise to the nets.
options: Correct: a comparison population without the nets controls for other causes.
More frequent sampling describes the same trend in more detail but cannot show what caused it.
Mosquito numbers can change for many reasons and do not show why kdr rose.
A stronger dose measures how resistant the mosquitoes are, not what made them resistant.

why.correct: (1.32 − 1.00) ÷ 2 thousand generations = 0.32 ÷ 2 = 0.16 per 1,000 generations. Between generations 20,000 and 40,000 the gain is (1.68 − 1.60) ÷ 20 = 0.004 per 1,000 generations, forty times slower.
Fitness gained 0.32 in the first 2,000 generations but only 0.08 in the last 20,000, and it was still rising at the end.
options: Correct: fast early gains, then slower but continuing gains.
The gain per 1,000 generations fell from 0.16 early to 0.004 late, so the rate was not steady.
The mean kept rising after generation 10,000, from 1.50 to 1.60 to 1.68.
The pattern is the reverse: the fastest gains came first.

why.correct: Because the ancestor is kept alive in the freezer, any later sample can compete against it head to head at the same time, in the same medium and temperature, so differences in growth reflect genetic change rather than different conditions.
options: Correct: a living ancestor allows a direct, side-by-side comparison.
The evolved populations carry new mutations that arose before freezing; freezing does not undo them.
Freezing is used to store whole samples, not to pick out fitter cells.
Generations happen only while cells grow; frozen cells do not reproduce.

why.correct: Intervals: 5,000 gives 1.39-1.49 and 40,000 gives 1.61-1.75, which do not overlap. 10,000 gives 1.45-1.55 and 20,000 gives 1.54-1.66, which overlap, so those two means are not shown to differ.
options: Correct: non-overlapping intervals at 5,000 and 40,000; overlapping ones at 10,000 and 20,000.
A higher mean is not enough; 10,000 (1.45-1.55) and 20,000 (1.54-1.66) overlap.
0 and 2,000 (1.00 and 1.28-1.36) do not overlap, and neither do 5,000 and 40,000.

why.correct: Twelve independent populations all improving in the same conditions points to natural selection by those conditions. Which beneficial mutations arose first was a matter of chance, so the genetic routes differed.
options: Correct: the same pressure, different chance mutations, the same outcome.
All 12 began from one cell, but they gained fitness through different new mutations that arose later.
Drift is random in direction; it would not raise fitness in all 12 populations.
Each population is transferred into its own flask, and the stem says the mutations mostly differed.

why.correct: Samples killing over 99% fell from 100% of samples to 1%, while the 70-99% type rose to about 70%. The least lethal type grew to 31% but never became the most common.
options: Correct: the extremely lethal type declined and the moderately lethal type took over.
Samples killing under 70% reached only 31%, and most samples still killed over 70% of lab rabbits.
The lab tests on never-exposed rabbits show the virus itself changed.
The most lethal type fell, from 100% to 1% of samples.

why.correct: The virus spreads only from living, infected rabbits through mosquito bites. A virus that kills its host within days has less time to be picked up, so moderately lethal types were passed on more and became common.
options: Correct: transmission favors virus that keeps its host alive and infectious longer.
Evolution has no goal; the change came from which viruses were transmitted more, not from what would benefit the virus later.
The most lethal types multiply fast within a rabbit; their problem is fewer chances to spread before the host dies.
The lab rabbits had never been exposed, so they were not selected for resistance.

why.correct: The standard strain did not change, so fewer deaths in wild rabbits given it must reflect a change in the rabbits: survivors of earlier outbreaks passed on resistance alleles.
options: Correct: the same virus kills fewer rabbits, so the rabbits changed.
This measures change in the virus, tested on never-exposed lab rabbits.
This also tracks the virus, not the wild rabbits.
This tracks the virus too; the lab rabbits did not change.

why.correct: By 1963 the rabbits had evolved resistance (standard-strain deaths fell from 90% to 30%), so they should survive the old virus better than 1951 rabbits did. A very lethal virus is still expected to kill many, since resistance is partial.
options: Correct: resistant rabbits do better, but resistance is partial.
The virus is unchanged, but the rabbits are not: they carry more resistance alleles.
Resistance is partial; 30% of 1963 rabbits still died from the milder standard strain.
Not meeting a virus does not remove resistance alleles; the 1963 rabbits descend from survivors.

why.correct: 10<sup>10</sup> particles × 1/10<sup>5</sup> = 10<sup>5</sup> = 100,000 resistant particles every day. A single drug therefore almost certainly meets resistant virus, which survives and multiplies.

The chance of carrying both independent mutations is 1/10<sup>5</sup> × 1/10<sup>5</sup> = 1/10<sup>10</sup>. 10<sup>10</sup> × 1/10<sup>10</sup> = 1 particle per day. Adding drug C makes it 1/10<sup>15</sup>, or about one particle every 100,000 days.

With one drug, about 100,000 resistant particles arise daily and take over. That large resistant population then produces mutants resistant to the next drug. Together, a particle must carry all three mutations at once, which the model predicts almost never happens.
options: Correct: one drug at a time lets resistance pile up mutation by mutation.
The reason is about resistance in the virus, not about the immune system.
The model treats the three drugs as working on their own; their benefit together comes from the multiplied odds.
Mutations arise at random whether or not a drug is present; the drug selects among them.

why.correct: Skipped doses let the virus multiply. Each copy is no more error-prone than before, but many more copies means many more chances for resistant mutants, which the drugs then select when levels rise again.

variables.name: Number of new virus particles made per day
variables.why: Low drug levels let the virus replicate, so many more particles are made.

variables.name: Chance that a particle resistant to all three drugs arises over the next year
variables.why: More copying means more mutations overall, so rare combinations, including triple resistance, become more likely.

variables.name: Share of new genomes carrying a given resistance mutation, before any selection
variables.why: The error rate of reverse transcriptase does not depend on the drugs; skipping doses changes how many copies are made, not how error-prone each copy is.

why.correct: Influenza's RNA genome is copied with many errors, so its surface proteins keep changing. People already immune to last year's forms are infected more easily by changed forms, so those spread. The vaccine is updated to match the forms expected to circulate.
options: Correct: mutation plus selection by population immunity keeps the virus changing.
New variants keep appearing; the strains are not a fixed set.
Immune memory from vaccination can last much longer; the virus changing is the main reason.
Vaccines do not cause mutations; mutations arise by chance during viral copying.

why.correct: Gene duplications are mutations that change the genome's structure. Plants with many EPSPS copies make much more enzyme, so some stays active despite glyphosate. Repeated spraying selected for these plants, and the genome change spread.
options: Correct: a duplication increased enzyme amount, and spraying selected for it.
Herbicides do not copy genes; duplications arise by chance, and spraying only selects among plants.
The data show more copies, not a changed enzyme; extra amount alone can explain survival.
The stem links copy number with survival across many farms, which this option ignores.

why.correct: Evolution is a change in the genetic makeup of a population over generations. Allele frequencies tracked over years and genomes compared across decades show it directly.
options: A change in allele frequency across generations is evolution, measured as it happens.
New mutations accumulating in a population's genomes over decades are evolution observed directly.
Individuals do not evolve; an insect becoming harder to kill during its life is not a genetic change in a population.
Fossils show evolution in the past, not change happening now.
No change is reported, so this observation shows no evolution.

why.correct: Singing males were found and parasitized more, so silent males lived longer and, despite having no song, mated enough to pass the mutation on. Its frequency rose fast because the pressure was strong.
options: Correct: lower attack rates gave silent males higher fitness.
The change is a mutation in a wing gene; learned habits are not inherited through DNA.
Flies select among males; they do not cause mutations.
Silent males cannot attract females by song; their advantage came from escaping the flies.

why.correct: Resistance is strongest exactly where toxin is highest, which fits reciprocal selection: toxic newts favor resistant snakes, and resistant snakes favor more toxic newts.
options: Correct: matched levels of toxin and resistance point to reciprocal selection.
No breeding by people is involved; the selection comes from the newts and snakes themselves.
The snakes do not make the toxin; they resist it.
Chance would not match resistance to toxin levels place by place.

why.correct: Replays from later samples could re-evolve citrate use and replays from earlier ones could not, so something changed in the population around generation 20,000 that made the later mutation work: history matters in evolution.
options: Correct: a first mutation made the population able to evolve citrate use later.
Replays from early samples also ran for many generations and still failed, so time alone was not the limit.
Revived cells mutate normally; they grew and evolved in the replays.
The ancestor could not use citrate in the presence of oxygen, and the flasks did not change.

why.correct: An outgroup is a taxon known from other evidence to lie outside the group being studied. Comparing with it shows which character states are older (present in the outgroup) and which are newer.
options: Correct: the outgroup is chosen because it lies outside the group studied.
Having many characters makes the oak a member of the group, not a reference outside it.
The moss shares the embryo character with the other land plants, so it belongs inside the group.
The fern is a member of the land-plant group; its place in the table does not make it a reference.

why.correct: Each character marks one clade: embryo (moss, fern, pine, oak), vascular tissue (fern, pine, oak), seeds (pine, oak). Nesting these groups gives moss branching first, then fern, with pine and oak as sister taxa; flowers then mark the oak branch alone.
options: Correct: the groups marked by the characters nest inside each other in this order.
Moss and fern share no character that pine and oak lack, so nothing groups them together.
Pine shares seeds with oak, not with the fern, so pine and fern are not sister taxa.
This reverses the nesting: the oak has every derived character, so it sits inside the most nested group.

why.correct: Embryo, seeds and flowers each need one change. Vascular tissue now needs two: no group on this tree contains exactly the fern, pine and oak, so vascular tissue must either arise twice (in the fern line and in the pine-oak line) or arise once in the ancestor of the four land plants and be lost in the moss. Total 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5, versus 4 for the tree in which the moss branches first. By maximum parsimony, the 4-change tree is preferred.
Seeds are found in pine and oak and in no other organism in the table, so they mark the ancestor that pine and oak alone share.
options: Correct: seeds are shared by pine and oak and lacking in the rest.
The fern has vascular tissue too, so it cannot separate pine and oak from the fern; within that group it is a shared ancestral character.
Every land plant in the table has it, so it does not group pine and oak apart from the fern.
Only the oak has flowers, so they do not unite the oak with the pine.

why.correct: A clade is an ancestor and all of its descendants. Fern-pine-oak (marked by vascular tissue) and pine-oak (marked by seeds) each include a common ancestor and every descendant of it.
options: A clade: the ancestor with vascular tissue and all of its descendants.
A clade: the seed plants descend from one ancestor that only they share.
Not a clade: the most recent ancestor of moss and fern is also the ancestor of pine and oak, which are left out.
Not a clade: their shared ancestor is the root, whose descendants include the other three plants.
Not a clade: it leaves out the fern, which descends from the same ancestor as pine and oak.

why.correct: Trace the mouse and the turtle back toward the root: the first node where their lines meet is node 2.
options: Node 1 is an ancestor of both, but not the most recent one; it also gave rise to the frog.
Correct: the lines from the mouse and the turtle first meet at node 2.
Node 3 is an ancestor of the turtle but not of the mouse.
Node 5 is the ancestor of the turtle, crocodile and sparrow only.

why.correct: The turtle's most recent common ancestor with the crocodile and with the sparrow is the same node, node 5, so it is equally related to both.
options: Correct: both pairs meet at node 5.
The crocodile meets the sparrow at node 6 but the lizard only at node 3, so it is closer to the sparrow.
The lizard meets the turtle at node 3, while the sparrow meets the turtle at node 5, a more recent ancestor, so the sparrow is the closer relative.
The frog is a living tip; it shares an ancestor (node 1) with the others but is not their ancestor.

why.correct: A clade contains a node and every tip descended from it. Node 6 gives crocodile and sparrow; node 5 gives turtle, crocodile and sparrow.
options: Node 6 and all of its descendants.
Node 5 and all of its descendants.
Not a clade: their shared ancestor, node 3, also gave rise to the sparrow, which is left out. The traditional group of reptiles is not a clade unless birds are included.
Not a clade: node 2 also gave rise to the turtle, crocodile and sparrow.
Not a clade: node 1 is their shared ancestor, and it gave rise to every animal on the tree.

why.correct: The skull feature is a shared derived character of crocodiles and birds, so it arose on the line between node 5 and node 6. A fossil that has it belongs on that line or within the group descended from node 6.
options: Correct: it shares the derived character that marks the crocodile-bird line.
Lizards and snakes lack the feature, so nothing links the fossil to them.
Turtles lack the feature; the turtle is no closer to the crocodile than to the sparrow.
Age alone does not place a fossil at the root; its characters show which line it belongs to.

why.correct: A clade must include every descendant of its common ancestor. Node 3 gave rise to the sparrow as well, so a group of its descendants without the sparrow is not a clade; the features named are older ones kept by some descendants and changed in birds.
options: Correct: leaving out a descendant of node 3 means the group is not a clade.
Birds do have scales on their legs; in any case, a clade must include every descendant of its ancestor.
Node 3 is their common ancestor, but it is also the ancestor of the sparrow, which the group leaves out.
Adding the mouse does not help: node 2 would then be the ancestor, and the sparrow would still be missing.

why.correct: Fewer differences mean a more recent common ancestor. Human-chimpanzee differ least (12), gorilla is 16 from both, orangutan 31 from all three, and macaque 62 from all four, so the groups nest in that order.
options: Correct: the smallest differences pair human and chimpanzee, then the others join in order.
Chimpanzee is 16 from gorilla but only 12 from human, so it pairs with human.
Human differs least from chimpanzee; the macaque differs most from every other primate.
Orangutan is 31 from gorilla but gorilla is only 16 from human and chimpanzee.

why.correct: Rate = 31 differences per 15 million years. Human-chimpanzee: 12 differences × (15 ÷ 31) = 5.8 million years ago. The same calibration gives about 7.7 million years for the gorilla split (16 × 15 ÷ 31).
The macaque differs from each ape at 62 positions. 62 × 15 ÷ 31 = 30 million years.
options: Correct: twice the orangutan's 31 differences means twice the time.
62 is the number of differences, not the time; it must be scaled by 15 ÷ 31.
15 million years is the orangutan split, which has only half as many differences.
This divides the time by two instead of doubling it.

why.correct: A molecular clock converts differences to time only if the rate of change is roughly constant across the lines compared; a line that changed faster would look older than it is.
options: Correct: a clock needs a roughly constant rate.
The region codes for no protein, which is useful: changes are mostly neutral and build up at a steadier rate.
Body size and habitat are not what the clock measures; only the rate of DNA change matters.
Visible characters can change at very different rates; the clock depends on the DNA changes.

why.correct: Selection removes most changes in a conserved gene, so fewer differences remain, but they still build up in proportion to time since each split. The branching order should match; the rate, and so the calibration, differs.
options: Correct: a slower clock, the same tree.
Mutations arise at similar rates, but in an essential gene most are removed by selection, so fewer differences remain.
Essential genes are copied just as accurately; they show fewer differences, not more.
Shared ancestry is the same whichever gene is read; a slower gene changes the counts, not the order.

why.correct: Two independent gains need 2 changes. One gain at the shared ancestor of mammals and reptiles needs that gain plus losses in the turtle line and in the lizard-snake line, 3 changes. Three separate gains need 3. The fewest changes means the trait evolved twice: convergent evolution, so the hearts are analogous in their four chambers.
options: Correct: 2 changes, the fewest possible.
One gain and two losses (turtle line and lizard-snake line) make 3 changes, more than needed.
Crocodiles and birds share an ancestor without the other groups, so one gain there explains both; three gains is 3 changes.
Mammals and reptiles last shared an ancestor over 300 million years ago and cannot interbreed.

why.correct: All living tips descend from the root through the same length of time. Branches can be rotated around any node, so which tip is drawn at the top carries no meaning.
options: Correct: tip order is arbitrary and all living taxa have evolved for the same time.
Trees show branching relationships, not a ladder from lower to higher.
Living tips sit at the present, the same distance in time from the root.
Tip order can be changed by rotating branches, so it says nothing about when lines appeared.

why.correct: R and P meet at the node joining P with (Q, R); R and S meet only at the root. A more recent common ancestor means a closer relationship.
options: Correct: R shares a more recent ancestor with P than with S.
Tips drawn next to each other are not necessarily close; R and S meet only at the root.
P meets Q at the node above (Q, R) but meets S only at the root, so P is closer to Q.
S is a living tip, not an ancestor; it shares the root with the others.

why.correct: Independent lines of evidence, DNA and fossil ankle bones, agreed on a new hypothesis, and the tree was revised. Phylogenies are tested and changed as evidence accumulates.
options: Correct: trees are hypotheses, revised by new evidence.
Here the fossils supported the DNA; molecular data include thousands of characters and often resolve conflicts.
Whales and hippos share a common ancestor; neither descends from the other's living species.
Shared habitat can produce similar body forms by convergence, which is why it is not used to group organisms.

why.correct: The first word of a scientific name is the genus. Lion and tiger share the genus Panthera; the house cat is in another genus of the same family.
options: Correct: same genus, Panthera.
Different genera: Panthera and Felis.
Different genera: Panthera and Felis.
Two of the three share a genus, so they are not equally related.

why.correct: The same bones in different forms are homologous: inherited from a common ancestor and modified as its descendants diverged into different ways of life.
options: Correct: shared bones modified in different directions.
The bones are the same set, inherited, not separately evolved; and the uses differ rather than match.
Bats, whales and humans do not exert selective pressure on each other.
The forms match their uses closely, which points to natural selection rather than chance.

why.correct: A character shared by every member of the group, and by its outgroup, is ancestral for that group; it cannot separate subgroups. Only characters that arose within the group can.
options: Correct: a shared ancestral character cannot sort members of the group.
Every mammal has a backbone, so it does not split them at all.
Backbones are inherited; they mark the larger group of vertebrates.
The backbone arose once, in an ancestor of all vertebrates.

why.correct: A state found in the outgroup is presumed ancestral; states found in some members of the group and not in the outgroup are derived and can mark clades.
options: Correct: the outgroup sets which states are old and which are new.
There is no minimum of six taxa; the outgroup's job is to tell old states from new.
The outgroup is a relative outside the group, not its ancestor.
Dating uses a calibrated molecular clock, not the outgroup's role in a cladogram.

why.correct: K × M pairs spawn (85%), fertilize (91%) and hatch (87%) about as well as the controls, but only 3% of the adult offspring are fertile: a postzygotic barrier, hybrid sterility.
options: Correct: the barrier appears only at the fertility stage.
85% of K × M pairs spawned, close to the 89-92% of the controls.
91% of K × M eggs were fertilized, about the same as in the controls.
87% of fertilized K × M eggs hatched, close to the controls.

why.correct: K and L interbreed and produce fertile offspring (96%), so by the biological species concept they are one species. M produces almost no fertile offspring with either, so it is a second species.
options: M is reproductively isolated from K and L: its hybrids are nearly all sterile.
Correct: K with L is one species; M is another.
K and L produce fertile offspring, so they are not separate species, even though they live 300 km apart.
The biological species concept is defined by interbreeding and fertile offspring, which is exactly what crosses test.

why.correct: In the shared streams, a L fish that spawned with M left mostly sterile offspring, so fish that avoided M left more fertile offspring. Over generations this strengthened a prezygotic barrier there (reinforcement). K never met M, so no such selection acted on K.
options: Correct: selection against hybrids where the two meet strengthens prezygotic isolation.
K fish do spawn with M readily, so not recognizing M is the opposite of what the data show.
L × L pairs spawn at 90%, so L fish are not reluctant to spawn in general.
K × M hybrids are 97% sterile, so K and M are different species too.

why.correct: Crosses within each population are controls: they show what the lab conditions give when no barrier exists. Without them, low spawning or fertility in mixed crosses could be blamed on the tanks.
options: Correct: the within-population crosses set the baseline.
Spawning and fertility rates do not measure genetic variation.
Within-population crosses produce no hybrids.
Where populations live is known from sampling, not from spawning rates in tanks.

why.correct: 1,000 × 0.91 fertilized = 910; × 0.87 hatched = 791.7; × 0.03 fertile = 23.75, about 24 fertile adults. Barriers multiply: even modest barriers at several stages add up to strong isolation.
A diploid parent's gamete carries n = 7; a tetraploid parent's gamete carries 28 ÷ 2 = 14. The zygote gets 7 + 14 = 21 chromosomes, three copies of each of the 7 kinds.

In meiosis I homologs pair and split two ways. With three of each, one cell gets two and the other one, at random for each of the 7 kinds, so nearly every gamete has a mixed, unbalanced set and fails.
options: Correct: uneven pairing in meiosis gives unbalanced gametes.
Mitosis copies each chromosome and splits the copies, which works with any number of sets; triploids grow normally.
The stem gives no evidence of a timing difference; the failure is in making gametes.
Sterility comes from chromosome number, not from particular alleles.

why.correct: Tetraploids breed among themselves (91% fertile offspring) but their hybrids with diploids are sterile (2%), so they are reproductively isolated: a new species by the biological species concept, formed in one step in the same place, which is sympatric speciation.
options: Correct: instant reproductive isolation in the same meadow.
Sharing a place does not make them one species; their hybrids are nearly all sterile.
The isolation arose in one generation, from one meiosis failure, in the same meadow.
The species status here rests on reproductive isolation shown by the crosses, not on appearance.

why.correct: Seeds form (15 per flower) and grow into triploids, which make almost no seed: a postzygotic barrier, hybrid sterility.
options: Correct: hybrid sterility of the triploids.
The stem says the two flower at the same time.
The stem says they are visited by the same bees; nothing suggests separate trips.
The table shows 15 seeds per flower in this cross.

why.correct: Y stays near 12 ribs for 4 million years, rises to about 18 within roughly 0.2 million years, then stays near 18: stasis broken by rapid change.
options: Correct: stasis, a quick change, then stasis again.
Steady change throughout is the gradual pattern, gradualism.
The total amount of change does not distinguish the two patterns; its timing does.
Ending higher is true of both lineages and says nothing about the timing of change.

why.correct: (20 − 10) ÷ 10 million years = 1.0 rib per million years. Lineage Y changes about 6 ribs in 0.2 million years during its jump, roughly 30 ribs per million years, but almost nothing the rest of the time.

Punctuated equilibrium proposes that change is concentrated around speciation, often in small populations where selection and drift act fast, and that established species then change little because stabilizing selection holds them near an optimum.
options: Correct: rapid change around speciation, stasis after.
Mutations occur all the time; stasis reflects selection keeping a form steady, not a lack of mutation.
The trait keeps varying and being inherited; it just stays near one mean.
Steady change would give the slope seen in lineage X, not flat stretches and a jump.

why.correct: If dense layers spanning the jump show intermediate rib numbers over a long time, the change was gradual but hidden by a gap; if they show a quick shift, the jump is real.
options: Correct: fill in the possible gap where the jump happens.
More shells per layer tighten each mean but cannot show what happened between layers.
Lineage X is a separate lineage; its pattern says nothing about gaps in Y's record.
Living snails show today's form, not the timing of a change millions of years ago.

why.correct: Separation stops gene flow; without it, each side evolves on its own; the differences that accumulate include reproductive barriers, so the populations stay separate species even when they meet again.

Flies meet mates on their own host fruit (habitat) and are active at different times (temporal), so few matings happen between the groups, even in the same place. This is a likely case of sympatric speciation in progress.
options: Correct: different hosts and different timing reduce mating between the groups.
Nothing in the stem describes hybrids or their fertility.
Nothing suggests reproductive parts or gametes are incompatible.
The stem says the trees grow side by side.

why.correct: The body parts used in mating do not fit together, so mating fails before any zygote forms: mechanical isolation, a prezygotic barrier.
options: Correct: a physical mismatch of reproductive parts.
The snails may attempt to mate; the problem is the fit of body parts, not signals.
No sperm reach the egg, so gamete compatibility is never tested.
No hybrids form, so their survival does not arise.

why.correct: In the lab the gametes are mixed directly, so timing and habitat play no part. If the binding proteins do not match, sperm cannot fuse with eggs: gametic isolation, a prezygotic barrier.
options: Correct: mismatched binding proteins block fertilization.
If binding fails, no zygote forms, so there are no embryos to die.
Sharing water does not overcome a mismatch between the sperm protein and the egg receptor.
Researchers mixed the gametes themselves, so release timing cannot be the barrier here.

why.correct: The barrier appears only in the second hybrid generation, after the first hybrids reproduce: hybrid breakdown, a postzygotic barrier.
options: Correct: the problem shows up in the hybrids' offspring.
The first hybrids are fertile, so this is not hybrid sterility.
The first hybrids survive and are healthy.
Fertilization works, since hybrids are produced.

why.correct: Adaptive radiation follows an opportunity: many open niches and isolated populations. Selection on different islands and foods drove beaks apart, and reproductive barriers arose between the descendants.
options: Correct: open niches plus isolation led to many species.
Changes acquired during an individual's life are not inherited.
The founders were few birds of one kind; the many species formed later.
Selection continued: beaks closely match each species' food, which chance alone does not explain.

why.correct: The biological species concept needs interbreeding to be tested, which is impossible for fossils and meaningless for asexual organisms. Body form, the morphological species concept, is used instead.
options: Correct: interbreeding cannot be tested in these cases.
Here interbreeding is known, so the biological species concept applies directly.
Behavior in the wild matters for the biological species concept; this is a case it handles, with care.
DNA data are usually used to support either concept; they do not force the morphological one.

why.correct: Prezygotic barriers act before a zygote forms. Different songs (behavioral) and different flowering months (temporal) keep mating from happening at all.
options: Behavioral isolation: no mating, no zygote.
Temporal isolation: no pollination between them.
Hybrid sterility acts after a zygote forms (postzygotic).
Hybrid inviability is postzygotic.
Hybrid breakdown is postzygotic.

why.correct: By the biological species concept, populations are separate species when they cannot interbreed and produce fertile offspring. A test of interbreeding shows whether reproductive isolation has evolved.
options: Correct: it tests reproductive isolation directly.
Geographic separation stops gene flow but does not by itself make them different species.
Allele frequencies differ between many populations of one species.
Different diets do not show whether the squirrels can still interbreed.

why.correct: Variety H plants were 58% infected when grown alone but 9% in mixed fields. R stayed near 3-4% either way.
options: Correct: 58% alone versus 9% in mixtures.
R was 4% infected alone and 3% in mixtures, about the same.
H infection fell from 58% to 9%, a large drop.
R's infection stayed low in mixed fields, so it kept its resistance.

why.correct: (58 − 9) ÷ 58 × 100 = 49 ÷ 58 × 100 = 84.5%, which rounds to 84% (85% also accepted). The drop is in the share of plants infected, not a drop of 49%.

In a uniform field, every neighbor is a host, so the fungus spreads plant to plant. In the mixture, susceptible plants are spaced apart by resistant ones, so many spores are wasted and the outbreak grows more slowly.
options: Correct: resistant neighbors break the chain of spread.
The stem describes a resistance allele, not a chemical; and R's own infection data do not suggest one.
Alleles are not passed between neighboring plants through their roots.
Nothing in the setup says planting dates differed; the fields were compared in the same outbreak year.

why.correct: Intervals: H alone 3.7-4.5; R alone 5.7-6.3; mixed 6.1-6.7. Mixed and H alone do not overlap, so they differ; mixed and R alone overlap, so a difference is not shown.
options: Correct: no overlap with H alone; overlap with R alone.
The mixed (6.1-6.7) and R-alone (5.7-6.3) intervals overlap.
R alone (5.7-6.3) and H alone (3.7-4.5) do not overlap, so they differ.
H alone does not overlap either of the others.

why.correct: A field of one genotype has no individuals that resist the new strain, so it can spread through the whole field. Mixed fields keep some H plants the new strain cannot infect, and H-alone fields resist it.
options: Correct: a uniform field of a now-susceptible genotype is the most vulnerable.
The new strain cannot infect H, so mixed fields keep some unaffected plants and spaced-out hosts.
Last year's strain is not this year's; the new strain cannot infect H.
The strain can infect only one of the two varieties, so plantings differ in how many hosts they offer.

why.correct: Heterozygosity rose from 0.16 to 0.29, heart defects fell from 21% to 4% and kinked tails from 88% to 18%, as the population grew from about 26 to 120 adults.
options: Correct: more variation, fewer defects.
Heterozygosity rose and defects fell.
Both heterozygosity and defects changed a great deal.
Heterozygosity had already risen by 2000-2004, when defects first fell.

why.correct: With few mates available, cats were often related, so kittens more often received the same recessive allele from both parents (inbreeding). Recessive defects then appear, and heterozygosity falls.
options: Correct: inbreeding exposes harmful recessive alleles.
Mutation rate per gene does not depend on population size; the issue is how alleles are combined.
Every kitten has the same set of genes; low heterozygosity means fewer different alleles, not fewer genes.
The defects are inherited and fell after new alleles arrived, which stress would not explain.

why.correct: Kittens born in the same years share the same habitat. If those descended from the released females have fewer defects than those that do not, the difference can be traced to the new alleles rather than to conditions.
options: Correct: same years and place, different ancestry.
Birth numbers say nothing about which kittens have defects or why.
This describes the source population, not whether its alleles caused the change here.
Area alone cannot separate the effect of habitat from the effect of new alleles.

why.correct: Surviving a new disease depends on some individuals carrying alleles that resist it. A small population with low heterozygosity has fewer different alleles, so the chance that some cats resist is lower, and one outbreak could wipe it out.
options: Correct: low variation makes a population vulnerable.
A small population can still pass a virus among its members, and losing cats matters more when there are few.
Cats differ genetically in how they respond to infection; that variation is what the period comparison is about.
Inbreeding lowers variation, including in immune genes; it does not strengthen immunity.

why.correct: Where malaria is common, survival is 92% for HbA HbS and 80% for HbA HbA. Where it is rare, both are 97%: the carrier advantage depends on malaria.
options: Correct: 92% versus 80% with malaria, 97% versus 97% without.
Where malaria is rare, the two genotypes survive equally (97%).
The advantage exists only where malaria is common.
Carriers survive better than HbA HbA where malaria is common.

why.correct: Heterozygote advantage: selection removes HbS in HbS HbS children and HbA through malaria deaths of HbA HbA children. Carriers, with the highest survival, pass on both alleles, so both persist (balancing selection).
options: Correct: the heterozygote has the highest fitness where malaria is common.
New mutations to HbS are far too rare to keep the allele at such high frequencies.
Infections do not change a person's alleles; mutations are random.
Dominance does not make an allele spread; in fact the disease is recessive.

why.correct: q = 0.10, so p = 0.90. Carriers: 2pq = 2 × 0.90 × 0.10 = 0.18, or 18%. HbS HbS newborns: q² = 0.01, 1%. Carriers hold one HbS allele each (0.18) and affected children two (2 × 0.01 = 0.02), so about 9 times as many HbS alleles are in carriers as in affected children.
The HbS allele was kept common by malaria. Without it the carrier advantage disappears, so the allele slowly declines, while mutation rate and the severity of the disease itself do not change.

variables.name: Frequency of the HbS allele
variables.why: Without malaria, carriers no longer survive better than HbA HbA, while HbS HbS children still rarely survive, so selection now removes HbS.

variables.name: Survival of HbA HbA children
variables.why: Their main extra risk, malaria, is gone, so their survival rises toward the 97% of the malaria-rare region.

variables.name: Rate at which new HbS mutations arise
variables.why: Mutation is random and does not depend on whether malaria is present.

variables.name: Survival of HbS HbS children
variables.why: Without medical care, sickle cell disease is just as severe; the graph shows similar low survival (18% and 22%) in both regions.

why.correct: Plants grown from cuttings are genetically identical. With no variation, there are no plants carrying resistance alleles to survive, so one pathogen strain threatens the whole crop. An earlier variety, the Gros Michel, was lost the same way in the 1950s.
options: Correct: a monoculture of clones has no variation for resistance.
Propagating by cuttings does not raise the mutation rate; it prevents new combinations of alleles.
The problem is that the plants are identical, not that they came from cuttings as such.
Nothing links flavor genes to fungal infection; the risk comes from uniformity.

why.correct: If plantings with more varieties suffered less under the same weather and the same pathogen, then variation among plants, not weather alone, made the difference.
options: Correct: a comparison that holds weather and pathogen constant while varying genetic variety.
Wet weather explains why the mold spread, not why one variety was hit so uniformly.
High earlier yields are why one variety was grown; they do not show why the loss was so large.
Where the mold came from does not show why the losses were so complete.

why.correct: The allele existed in Europe long before HIV reached people there. Variation already in a population can, by chance, include disease resistance to a pathogen it has never met, which is why genetic variation helps populations survive new threats.
options: Correct: existing variation can contain resistance to new threats.
The allele is far older than the HIV epidemic; mutations are not caused by need.
Resistance protects the person who carries it; a population with more variation is more likely to have survivors.
Genetic variation affects survival of new diseases in any population, human or not.

why.correct: Vulnerability comes from low genetic variation: clones and small, inbred populations have few different alleles, so they are unlikely to include individuals that resist a new disease.
options: Genetically identical clones: one susceptible genotype.
Small and inbred: few alleles to draw on.
Large and exchanging genes with other populations: high variation.
Large, outcrossing and widespread: high variation.
Large and sexually reproducing: high variation.

why.correct: Variation in molecules means each population can carry the forms of an enzyme that work best where it lives, and the species as a whole can shift as temperatures change.
options: Correct: molecular variation matched to local conditions.
A fish cannot change the alleles it inherited; frequencies differ between populations.
The allele is common in one region and rare in the other, which dominance alone would not produce.
Heterozygotes make two forms of the enzyme, not necessarily twice the amount.

why.correct: Modern crops are often genetically narrow. Old and wild varieties keep alleles, for example for disease resistance or heat tolerance, that can be bred into crops when a new threat appears.
options: Correct: stored variation is insurance against new threats.
Old varieties usually yield less; they are stored for their alleles, not to replace crops.
Seeds in storage are kept dormant and change very little; their value is the alleles they already have.
Planting one variety everywhere is what makes crops vulnerable.

why.correct: More genetic variation means more different alleles and combinations, so it is more likely that some individuals happen to carry traits that let them survive the new conditions.
options: Correct: more variation, more chance of survivors.
Few alleles make survivors less likely.
Clones share one genotype, so a change that kills one may kill all.
Two founders carry at most four alleles of each gene.

why.correct: Glycine rose by 2.0 µmol on day 1 but only 0.1 on day 7; alanine followed the same shape at about half the amount. Without sparks, no glycine formed at all.
options: Correct: fast early rise, leveling off, glycine above alanine.
Alanine stayed below glycine on every day.
The no-spark flasks had no glycine at any time.
The daily increase shrank from 2.0 to 0.1 µmol, so the rate was not steady.

why.correct: (3.6 − 0) ÷ 2 days = 1.8 µmol per day. From day 5 to day 7 the rate was (6.5 − 6.1) ÷ 2 = 0.2 µmol per day.

The control flasks match the experimental ones in every way except the sparks, and no amino acids appeared in them. So the sparks' energy, not microbes or the gases left to themselves, produced the amino acids.
options: Correct: the only difference is the sparks, and only sparked flasks made amino acids.
No amino acids formed in the controls, so nothing was there to break down.
A control in the lab cannot show what the air of the young Earth was made of.
The experiment tested amino acid formation, not protein synthesis.

why.correct: The flasks were sealed, so methane, ammonia and hydrogen were not replaced. As they were converted, less was left to react and the rate of formation fell. (Sparks can also break some products down, adding to the leveling.)
options: Correct: reactants in a closed system are used up.
Nothing in the flasks was alive, and amino acids do not assemble into cells on their own.
The stem says sparks passed continuously.
Both amino acids kept rising slowly, so neither was converted into the other.

why.correct: To test the new hypothesis about the atmosphere, change the gases to match it while keeping everything else the same, and look for amino acids. (Such experiments give lower yields, which rise when the water is buffered against acid.)
options: Correct: test the gases that the new hypothesis proposes.
A longer run with the old gases does not test the new atmosphere.
Adding amino acids tests their stability, not whether they can form from these gases.
Letting in modern air adds oxygen, which the early atmosphere lacked.

why.correct: With clay, half the fatty acid formed vesicles in 0.9-1.0 min instead of 84-85 min, roughly 85 times faster, with or without RNA.
options: Correct: much faster, in both clay conditions.
The times fell from 85 min to about 1 min, so formation was faster, not slower.
Clay without RNA also sped formation (0.9 min).
Clay changed the formation time from 85 min to about 1 min.

why.correct: 48% ÷ 3% = 16 times as many vesicles held RNA when it was bound to clay.
The clay speeds vesicle formation on its surface, and the RNA is stuck to that same surface, so the growing membranes enclose clay particles together with their RNA.
options: Correct: membranes form where the RNA is, and enclose it.
The RNA was tagged and counted inside vesicles; nothing suggests the clay cut it up.
Fatty acids assemble on their own in water; no enzyme is needed.
Vesicles formed faster with clay, so fatty acids were not removed.

why.correct: Two separate steps, making polymers and enclosing them in a membrane, can be helped by the same mineral, so a single setting might bring them together. It is support for a hypothesis, not proof of where life began.
options: Correct: one setting could connect polymer formation and protocell formation.
Clay is not alive; it provides a surface that speeds reactions.
Lab results show what is possible, not where it happened; several settings remain possible.
Fatty acids are monomers of a kind, and the RNA here was already present.

why.correct: RNA stores information in a base sequence that can be copied, and ribozymes catalyze reactions, as in the ribosome.
options: Correct: RNA does both.
DNA stores information but does not catalyze reactions in cells.
Proteins catalyze reactions but cannot be copied by base pairing.
This takes two different molecules; the question asks for one that does both.

why.correct: If the first catalysts were RNA, the machine that makes proteins should still rely on RNA at its core, a molecular fossil of a time before proteins.
options: Correct: an RNA catalyst at the heart of protein synthesis.
Genetic information for proteins is in mRNA copied from DNA, not in rRNA.
The ribosome's rRNA joins amino acids; it does not fold finished proteins.
An RNA core in the ribosome points to RNA coming first, not DNA.

why.correct: Ribose's 2′ –OH helps break RNA chains in water; deoxyribose lacks it, and DNA's double strand allows repair from the partner strand. So DNA keeps long sequences intact, an advantage as genomes grew.
options: Correct: stability favors DNA for storage.
The table says DNA does not catalyze reactions in cells.
DNA has 4 bases; 20 building blocks describes proteins.
DNA is copied using a template, by base pairing.

why.correct: Copying with errors creates heritable variation; limited nucleotides create competition; variants that copy themselves better leave more copies. That is natural selection, which could have shaped the earliest replicators.
options: Correct: variation plus competition plus inheritance gives selection.
The stem says copying makes errors, so copies vary.
Ribozymes copy RNA; nothing in the setup makes DNA.
Most errors leave a working molecule or one slightly worse; selection sorts among them.

why.correct: 3.5 ÷ 4.6 × 100 = 76%. Life left evidence within about the first billion years, so its origin was fairly quick on a geological scale.
Comparing the ancient structures with ones forming today points to microbial mats as their builders, so life existed by then.
options: Correct: similar structures, built by similar microbial mats.
Oxygen did not build up in the air until about 2.4 billion years ago.
Mounds show where mats lived then, not where life first arose.
Many rock layers form without life, which is why fine, mound-shaped layers are the key feature.

why.correct: Early Earth had almost no free oxygen and was shaped by volcanoes and impacts. Oxygen and the ozone layer came much later, from photosynthesis.
options: True: free oxygen built up only after about 2.4 billion years ago.
True: volcanic outgassing and impacts were common.
Ozone forms from oxygen, which was scarce, so ultraviolet light reached the surface.
Land plants appeared over 4 billion years later than Earth formed, far after life began.
Before life, organic molecules had to form without cells.

why.correct: Joining monomers is dehydration synthesis: it releases water. In open water the reverse, hydrolysis, wins. Surfaces that bind and concentrate monomers, or drying that removes water, tip the balance toward chains.
options: Correct: concentration and drying favor dehydration synthesis.
Hydrolysis breaks chains; adding water works against polymer formation.
Free oxygen was scarce, and these joining reactions do not use it.
Monomers must come close together to join.

why.correct: At vents, hot water full of dissolved minerals and gases meets cold seawater, creating chemical gradients that supply energy and metal-rich surfaces that can catalyze reactions, while deep water shields against ultraviolet light and impacts.
options: Correct: energy from chemical gradients and catalytic minerals.
Deep-sea vents are dark; sunlight does not reach them.
Early oceans had little free oxygen.
Vent water is hot, which can also break RNA; that is one argument against vents.

why.correct: Each step needs the one before: monomers from simple molecules, polymers from monomers, protocells from polymers inside membranes, and finally the DNA-RNA-protein system of modern cells.
Early Earth had no free oxygen and no life. Today oxygen reacts with and breaks down organic molecules, and microbes everywhere would eat any new ones long before they could assemble into anything.
options: Correct: oxygen and existing life destroy new organic molecules.
The laws of chemistry are the same; the conditions differ.
Lightning and volcanoes still occur.
Organisms do not have such chemicals; the issue is oxygen and consumption by existing life.
